items.stem: Which topic is explicitly listed among standard transplant discharge education subjects?

options.text: Signs and symptoms of infection
DonorNet refusal code entry
KDPI calculation variables
Independent living donor advocate credentialing

explanation.rationale_correct: Discharge education curricula explicitly include signs and symptoms of infection alongside rejection recognition, medications, follow-up testing, and self-monitoring at home.

rationale_incorrect.B: DonorNet refusal documentation is a program/UNOS operational task, not a standard patient discharge education topic.
rationale_incorrect.C: KDPI is an allocation metric for clinicians and policy, not a listed discharge teaching subject.
rationale_incorrect.D: Independent donor advocate roles are part of living donation evaluation, not the discharge education topic list for recipients.

items.stem: You are the transplant coordinator reviewing infection-prevention handouts before a home visit. A 55-year-old solid-organ transplant patient is the focus of today's interaction. Education was started during the waiting period and continues after listing. The team wants teaching aligned with standard references before documentation is finalized. When explaining why living donor organs may offer advantages over some deceased-donor options, which donor characteristic should the coordinator emphasize?

options.text: The organ is typically from a young healthy person who completed an intensive medical evaluation
Living donors are never medically evaluated before donation
Deceased-donor organs always function better than any living-donor organ
Living donation eliminates the need for any immunosuppression after transplant

explanation.rationale_correct: Living donor transplant benefits include an organ from a typically young healthy person who has undergone an intense medical evaluation.

rationale_incorrect.B: Living donors undergo intensive medical evaluation before donation.
rationale_incorrect.C: Living donor organs may offer advantages related to donor health and timing rather than deceased donors always functioning better.
rationale_incorrect.D: Recipients still require immunosuppression after living donor transplantation.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 7, Care of Living Donors → Introduction → 6.a.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: organ is from a (typically) young healthy person who has undergone an intense medical evaluation

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 7 → Introduction → 6.a. (living donor organ from evaluated healthy donor); PDF p. 331 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

items.notes: Scenario companion (wave 3) paired with cctc-1044. Source-first item. Sixth 010400 item; living-donor quality advantage distinct from pulmonary rehab (cctc-1035) and health-maintenance screening (cctc-1020); anchor verified on Cupples p. 331.

items.stem: A coordinator is revising the post-discharge call guide for recipients and caregivers. Evaluate the following statements about when to contact the transplant team:

elements.text: Medication refill requests are examples of non-urgent matters.
Signs and symptoms of rejection are urgent matters.
General concerns about diet, activity, and exercise are urgent matters.
Shortness of breath is an urgent matter.

options.text: I and II only
I, II, and IV only
II and III only
I, II, III, and IV

explanation.rationale_correct: Medication refills and similar routine needs are non-urgent, while rejection symptoms, infection concerns, chest pain, and shortness of breath require urgent outreach. General diet and activity questions are explicitly non-urgent.

rationale_incorrect.A: Statement IV is also true—shortness of breath is listed as urgent.
rationale_incorrect.C: Statement III is false; diet and exercise questions are non-urgent.
rationale_incorrect.D: Statement III is false; not all four statements are correct.

primary_anchor.quote_hint: Non-urgent matters may include Medication refills … Urgent matters may include Signs and symptoms of rejection … Shortness of breath

items.stem: When counseling a transplant candidate about pretransplant immunizations, why is early vaccination emphasized in standard references?

options.text: Vaccine response may be diminished with organ failure and further reduced after immunosuppression
All live vaccines are preferred immediately after transplantation
Immunizations are unnecessary before transplant if the candidate feels well
Post-transplant vaccines always produce stronger immunity than pretransplant doses

explanation.rationale_correct: Candidates and recipients are at increased infection risk; response to many vaccines is diminished in organ failure, and transplant recipients may have suboptimal vaccination responses due to immunosuppression, so immunizations should be updated before transplantation when possible.

rationale_incorrect.B: Live vaccines require careful timing and are generally avoided after transplant rather than preferred immediately.
rationale_incorrect.C: Early immunization is emphasized because organ failure and later immunosuppression reduce vaccine response.
rationale_incorrect.D: Post-transplant vaccination responses are often suboptimal rather than stronger than pretransplant immunization.

primary_anchor.quote_hint: response to many vaccines is diminished in organ failure … suboptimal response to vaccinations due to their immunosuppressed status … update immunizations prior to transplantation

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 5 → Immunizations → A.2.–4. (diminished vaccine response with organ failure/immunosuppression; update before transplant); PDF p. 180 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

items.notes: Source-first item. Pretransplant vaccine-response angle distinct from live-vaccine interval (cctc-1077) and post-transplant restart timing (cctc-3074); anchor verified on Cupples p. 180.

items.stem: When a transplant program declines a deceased-donor kidney offer presented through DonorNet, what documentation must be provided to UNOS?

options.text: A reason or refusal code
No documentation when the surgeon verbally declines
Documentation only for accepted offers
A refusal code only when the candidate is permanently inactive

explanation.rationale_correct: Whenever a deceased-donor kidney offer is declined, a reason or refusal code must be provided to UNOS even though the accepting physician makes the final decision.

rationale_incorrect.B: Verbal decline without coded documentation does not meet UNOS reporting requirements.
rationale_incorrect.C: Declined offers require refusal documentation, not only accepted offers.
rationale_incorrect.D: Refusal codes are required for declined offers regardless of candidate inactive status.

items.stem: After a deceased-donor allocation match run, the allocating OPO must report organ offer outcomes to the OPTN. According to OPTN policy, within what timeframe must the OPO submit this report?

options.text: Within 30 days of the match run date
Within 90 days after waitlist registration only
By recipient hospital discharge or 42 days after transplant, whichever is first
Within 1 day of every routine medication refill request

explanation.rationale_correct: OPTN Policy 18.3 requires OPOs to report the outcomes of organ offers to the OPTN within 30 days of the match run date. Allocating OPOs and transplant hospitals that received offers share responsibility for accurate outcome reporting.

rationale_incorrect.B: Ninety days after waitlist registration applies to Transplant Candidate Registration (TCR), not organ-offer outcome reporting.
rationale_incorrect.C: Discharge or 42 days after transplant is the timely collection window for transplant recipient registration (TRR), not organ-offer outcomes.
rationale_incorrect.D: Medication refill requests are not the trigger for organ-offer outcome reporting.

items.stem: You are the transplant coordinator covering the afternoon clinic line. A 52-year-old kidney recipient discharged six weeks ago calls from work. He feels well, takes medications on schedule, and reports no fever, pain, or urinary changes. He only wants to confirm whether his follow-up visit is next Tuesday at 10 a.m. as discussed at discharge. The on-call surgeon asks you to document how this contact should be triaged. How should this contact be categorized?

options.text: An urgent matter requiring immediate after-hours contact
A non-urgent matter such as appointment verification
An emergency that requires activating local EMS before notifying the team
A matter that should wait until the next unscheduled clinic visit

explanation.rationale_correct: Verification of appointment date and time is explicitly listed as a non-urgent reason to contact the transplant team. Coordinators teach recipients to distinguish routine questions from urgent clinical changes.

rationale_incorrect.A: Urgent matters include infection symptoms, rejection signs, wound drainage, chest pain, shortness of breath, bleeding, and stroke symptoms—not routine scheduling questions.
rationale_incorrect.C: Routine appointment confirmation does not constitute a local EMS emergency.
rationale_incorrect.D: Non-urgent matters are still appropriate to address through normal team communication channels rather than deferred indefinitely.

primary_anchor.quote_hint: Non-urgent matters may include verification of appointment date and time

items.stem: When a candidate is listed in the UNOS candidate database (UNet), which candidate information is entered as part of standard waitlist registration data?

options.text: Blood type, height, weight, and other clinical variables
Only the candidate's personal social media identifiers
Only post-transplant discharge medication schedules
Only the surgeon's operative note from a prior unrelated surgery

explanation.rationale_correct: Waitlist registration in UNet includes candidate blood type, height, weight, and other clinical variables used for allocation matching.

rationale_incorrect.B: UNet registration uses clinical and demographic listing variables, not social media identifiers.
rationale_incorrect.C: Discharge medication schedules are post-transplant care documents, not primary UNet listing fields.
rationale_incorrect.D: Prior unrelated operative notes are not the described UNet candidate registration data set.
